extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in automated theorem proving, formal verification, and ML-for-code (LLM-based provers)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, using, and evaluating a small benchmark (miniCodeProps) of Lean 4 program properties to measure and compare automated theorem provers' ability to generate proofs for code specifications. Covers dataset composition, formats, difficulty labeling, and evaluation modes (full-proof and tactic-by-tactic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-contained, simple program properties
rubrics_metrics.description: miniCodeProps contains 201 specifications about lightweight, self-contained programs (e.g., lists, natural numbers, binary trees) with varied proof difficulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benchmark items should be simple, self-contained code blocks and properties (not large, complex repositories) so that models' core proving capabilities can be isolated and evaluated. The authors explicitly filter out primarily mathematical-induction files and translate TIP Haskell programs into Lean 4 focusing on programming-style properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum level of competency
rubrics_metrics.description: Properties are intended to represent a “minimum level of competency” for automated neural theorem provers — analogous to interview-style self-contained exercises for software engineers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include medley properties that test standard induction and 1–2 library theorems; benchmark should expose whether a system has basic inductive proof capability in program verification contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property categorization / difficulty splits
rubrics_metrics.description: Properties are grouped into Medley (easy), Termination (medium), and Sorting (hard) splits; the benchmark classifies each property by primary subject matter and difficulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the three-category split to analyze performance by difficulty and subject (lists/nats/trees; lemmas supporting termination; nonstandard sorting algorithms). Table 1 shows counts per category; difficulty indicates expected proof length/effort (medley: few lines; termination/sorting: tens of lines/hours).

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty heuristic (score field)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each property carries an integer score in the range [1–5] used as a difficulty heuristic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this numeric difficulty label as an auxiliary measure when analyzing model performance; authors use it in dataset records (see Table 2, 'score').

rubrics_metrics.name: Include termination lemmas
rubrics_metrics.description: Benchmark includes 28 lemmas that support termination proofs for recursive functions; termination proofs are required in Lean 4 for recursive definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because recursive functions must be paired with termination proofs, include termination lemmas (often difficult and time-consuming for humans) to test practical aspects of ITP automation. The benchmark intentionally includes human-produced termination lemmas with proofs removed to measure difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide code dependencies (deps)
rubrics_metrics.description: The underlying code block (dependencies) for a property is typically necessary to complete proofs, so models are always provided with the code dependencies ('deps' in the dataset).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dataset items must include all definitions/lemmas required to define the property so model prompts include the necessary context. Table 2 shows the 'deps' text and 'file_locs' indicating exact file lines to append.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset format and fields
rubrics_metrics.description: The benchmark is formatted as a jsonlines file; each item contains fields such as full_name, prop_defn, prop_loc, score, deps, proof_state, and file_locs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the initial proof state ('proof_state') and file locations ('file_locs') so proof-by-proof and tactic-by-tactic evaluations can reconstruct the environment. See Table 2 for an example record layout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial proof state provided
rubrics_metrics.description: Each benchmark item includes the initial proof state of the property (the context and goal at the start of the proof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing the initial proof state enables tactic-by-tactic methods where the model is given the current proof state and must propose the next tactic; include variables and goal in the state as text (see example in Table 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation modes: full-proof generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Full-proof generation: the model generates entire proof candidates (full proofs) given the deps and the property, and candidates are checked by the Lean 4 kernel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure success using pass@k (authors use pass@32: generate 32 candidates, success if at least one passes the verifier). Authors used GPT-4o and also a refinement variant (many-to-one) that takes previous failed candidates and attempts to generate improved proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation modes: tactic-by-tactic generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Tactic-by-tactic generation: model is given the current proof state (and context) and returns suggestions for the next tactic; each suggestion is applied and the resulting proof state is used to prompt for the next tactic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow common best-first search procedures for tactic generation. Input format should include the dependent code, the property being proven, and the history of generated tactics. Use a tactic model trained to accept (context, proof state) inputs (e.g., ntp-ctx-1.3B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof verification by Lean 4 kernel
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof candidates (full proofs or tactic sequences) are checked by the Lean 4 kernel; a property is considered proven only if the kernel accepts the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on the ITP's kernel as ground-truth verifier; do not accept syntactic-looking proofs without kernel verification. The evaluation code publicly released runs the Lean 4 verifier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success metric: pass@k and refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use pass@k (e.g., pass@32) to report how many properties have at least one successful proof among k generated candidates. Refinement can be used as a technique by feeding failed candidates back to the model and requesting improved proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors used k=32 for base generation and a refinement variant that, when initial 32 candidates fail, provides those 32 to the model and samples k=16 new generations per refinement round for T=2 rounds; this outperformed sampling 64 candidates without refinement in their tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search algorithm for tactic generation: best-first
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt the de-facto standard algorithm for tactic generation: best-first search over tactic suggestions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine tactic proposals from the model with a search strategy (best-first) that prioritizes promising proof states. Use trained tactic models that accept context+proof state to generate proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benchmark size and tractability tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: miniCodeProps is intentionally fairly small (201 properties) because evaluating theorem-proving models requires many calls to language models and is time-consuming/expensive for large datasets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep benchmark small enough to permit extensive evaluation (search, many samples, refinement) yet representative of the target distribution; authors argue the set is sufficient to 'break' current methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sourcing and translation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Source properties from a recognized corpus (Tons of Inductive Problems, TIP) and translate programs from Haskell into Lean 4; filter out items primarily about mathematical induction to focus on program verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using an existing corpus provides relevance to the verification community and preserves varied property types; manual translation is used to ensure correct Lean 4 encodings and to include necessary termination lemmas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative examples and human-readable proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide illustrative examples (e.g., zip over concatenation, non-standard insertion) with example proofs (correct and incorrect) to explain what makes items interesting/difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include example GPT-generated proofs (both successful and incorrect) to reveal typical model behaviors (unnecessary simplifier args, placeholders, invalid induction) and to guide future method development and error analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure range of proving abilities across splits
rubrics_metrics.description: Report per-split performance (Medley / Termination + Sorting / Overall) to characterize where models succeed or fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors report percentages proven for each split and overall; use these breakdowns to identify which capabilities (basic induction vs. termination reasoning vs. complex algorithm proofs) remain challenging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide file-level reconstruction info (file_locs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include file_locs listing the last line in each file needed to define the property so evaluators can reconstruct the environment by appending files up to those lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This facilitates deterministic environment reconstruction for the verifier and for tactic-by-tactic interactions where the kernel needs complete definitions.
